stories.title: Boy killed and man injured after train hits car in Mayo
stories.summary: A 12-year-old boy has died following a collision between a train and a car in Co Mayo last night. The boy and a man in his late 40s were travelling in a car when the collision occurred at a user-operated level crossing at Kiltybo, near Ballyhaunis, in Co Mayo, shortly before 9pm. The man was taken to hospital by ambulance for treatment. His injuries are described as not life-threatening. The level crossing runs across a secondary road that intersects with the N60, which is situated a short distance away. Following the crash, all passengers on the train safely disembarked and onward transport was arranged. Iarnród Éireann said "our thoughts are with everyone affected".

stories.title: EPA investigating noise complaints at Dublin data centre
stories.summary: An investigation is under way by the Environmental Protection Agency into complaints about noise emitting from a new data centre in Clondalkin in west Dublin. The operator said it has applied mitigation measures and is continuing to investigate the issue. Concerns in west Dublin first arose in late July, when some residents living close to the new Echelon DUB10 data centre in the Clondalkin Industrial Estate began hearing an unusual noise. Residents had described a persistent humming, primarily at night but also during the day. After receiving a number of complaints about the noise, the EPA launched an investigation which it said is still under way. Aaron Jeffrey, who lives more than 2km away from the data centre said that when the issue began in late summer he thought it was his imagination, or a noise that was occurring within his home, but he soon realised he was not alone.

stories.title: Byrne confident of EU budget deal under Irish presidency
stories.summary: Minister for European Affairs Thomas Byrne has said he is "absolutely confident" that agreement can be reached on the next long-term EU budget before Ireland's Presidency of the EU concludes at the end of the year. European Affairs Ministers are meeting in Dublin today and tomorrow as talks on the next long-term EU budget reach a critical stage. One of the key aim's of Ireland's EU Presidency is to agree the budget, known as the multiannual financial framework (MFF), before the end of the year. However, several countries, including Germany, want to rein in spending. Speaking as he arrived at Dublin Castle for the meeting of the General Affairs Council, Mr Byrne stressed the urgency of the negotiations. "I'm absolutely confident we can achieve this by the end of the year because I think we need to, and the reason we need to is because we need to have the funds in place by the 1 January 2028.

stories.title: Volkswagen flags 50,000 more job cuts across car group
stories.summary: Shares in Volkswagen were up 7% in early trade in Frankfurt this morning after the supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker last night struck a major turnaround agreement that averted an escalation with ‌unions and shareholder Lower ⁠Saxony. The deal on the biggest restructuring in the group's 89-year history includes a further 50,000 job cuts, bringing the group's total to 100,000, and leaves open the future of four of its German plants. The transformation plan is an attempt to counter painful tariffs, overcapacity and aggressive Chinese rivals. The plan, the most extensive restructuring in Volkswagen's 89-year history, includes exploring alternatives for four German plants that will eventually run out of models during the next decade. It also averts a major clash with unions by putting the scenario of an extraordinary general meeting on the backburner, a scenario that was considered by management to push through its plans against workers and Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, Lower Saxony. The deal will result in a simplification of Volkswagen's conglomerate structure and limit the influence of the group's supervisory board - on which unions and Lower Saxony hold a majority - on key decisions.

stories.title: WMO warns El Niño could fuel extreme weather worldwide
stories.summary: The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says a potentially exceptional El Niño warming event is now firmly established in the tropical Pacific and is expected to strengthen significantly into a "very strong" El Niño over the coming months. The event could reshape rainfall and temperature patterns across large parts of the planet, increasing the risk of floods in some places, drought in others and additional extreme heat. The WMO says almost all land areas are likely to experience above-normal temperatures during the coming months. WMO forecasting centres put the probability of El Niño persisting through February 2027 at nearly 100%, a remarkable degree of certainty. It is the first time that an El Niño/La Niña update has been so unequivocal. The event is expected to continue intensifying through the autumn and peak towards the end of 2026, although its climatic effects are expected to continue well into 2027.

stories.title: Gaffney was an immense asset - a striker like no other
stories.summary: I was halfway through writing a column about tomorrow's FAI Cup game between St Patrick’s Athletic and Bohemians when an announcement came across my screen that made me change direction. The Pat's-Bohs game can wait. But to summarise - it’s a big game for both sides! Players are forgotten quickly enough in football and I think when someone like Rory finishes playing it’s important that a few words are written about the player he was, because his contribution to Shamrock Rovers over the last number of years went far beyond a goals column on a stats page. The biggest reason being that we were probably completely different types of strikers and there wasn’t a chance I was capable of doing some of the things he could do. I first remember properly playing against him in England in November 2019. Swindon against Walsall in League Two. Mine was my old reliable - arriving in the box and scoring from close range. Rory’s was completely different. A brave header where he attacked a ball knowing the goalkeeper was coming the opposite direction with fists raised and there was every chance he could have been decapitated in the process.

stories.title: Murray and Casey step away as Dublin joint managers
stories.summary: Dublin women's footballers are on the hunt for a new management team after Derek Murray and Paul Casey confirmed they will not be seeking a third term at the helm. Casey - an All-Ireland winner and eight-time Leinster SFC champions with the men - had previously served as a selector and defensive coach with the squad. Murray has been part of the management team since 2022. They guided the Dubs to All-Ireland glory in 2025, beating Meath the decider, and won two Leinster titles. In a statement released on Wednesday, Dublin LGFA said: "Derek Murray and Paul Casey have informed the executive committee of Dublin LGFA that they will not seek a third term as managers of the Dublin Ladies senior football team. "The executive committee would like to thank Derek and Paul most sincerely for their professionalism, dedication and enthusiasm during their term not only as senior managers but previously as key members of the Dublin senior management team. "Their service to Dublin has been incredible and we as a committee have been most fortunate to have had the privilege to work closely alongside both men. Derek and Paul are a credit to their clubs, Round Tower Clondalkin and Lucan Sarsfields.

stories.title: The Button Factory at 30 - keeping Dublin's music scene alive
stories.summary: At a time when hostility to Irish cultural venues sits at a peak, one Dublin haven remains intact. There's a general understanding that cultural institutions and venues tend to feel cold to the touch, only to become thawed by your attention. By contrast, everything within the Button Factory, which this year celebrates its third decade in business, has always felt warm. Inside, the four walls that frame it – lined with the names, awards and records it has helped, contributed to and encouraged – feel increasingly like refuge from a city that has spent the last ten years trading its artistic lineage for commercial prospects. Acting as a crucial bridge between the city we once knew and the one we’re now faced with, that it stands today at 30 feels less like an anniversary and more like a miracle. "People who come here have a certain amount of trust in the space," Finn McCarthy, venue coordinator at the Button Factory says. "Which tends to mean that whether you have a crowd of 550 or 185, the room feels full – even if that’s just of good will." Though the venue’s founding came in 1996, the story of the Button Factory – or Buttoner, for regulars – really starts in the 1980s. As Ireland reckoned a decade of recession, unemployment and emigration, Córas Iompair Éireann took it upon itself to buy a suite of dilapidated properties in Temple Bar to turn them into a central, underground bus station. As the plans were being drawn, the organisation offered available rooms as affordable, short term rentals to artists, creating unbeknownst to themselves something of a bohemian cultural hub. "Everyone was in a band in the 1980s, but no one had anywhere to practice or record," says Paddy Dunning, the Button Factory’s founder, and a former renter of the scheme. "So we built studios and rehearsal rooms from the things we could take for free from skips. Then, when we heard that the area was to be demolished to make a dirty, greasy bus station, we knew we had to do something." An alliance of 12, dubbed the Temple Bar Development Council, was quickly formed in an attempt to save the area. Together, they met with Paddy Teahon, then-assistant secretary of the Taoiseach's Department, and Charlie Haughey, then-Taoiseach, to share their belief of the area’s massive potential. Using Sheffield, a city which had recently been developed following the fall of the steel industry and had since become a cultural hub as a recent example, they managed to provide a convincing narrative. "As a result, we set up 23 cultural centres, saved many architecturally important buildings, created 1000s of jobs and saved hundreds of homes." While the area was being flipped, Dunning and his team moved their then-already well-respected studios, rehearsal spaces and storage – which had, at that stage, welcomed the likes of Van Morrison, Sinéad O’Connor and Spandau Ballet to record – to a space on Ormond Quay, where it thrived from 1991-95 as something of a community hub. "We had over 30,000sqft of rehearsal spaces, studios, cages for the bands and a 1000-capacity venue," Dunning says. "I still remember Louis Walsh calling me at the time to say he had no money but could this new band he was forming, called Boyzone, rehearse on credit." In 1996, the Temple Bar Music Centre was born, resplendent with an auditorium, rehearsal rooms, a college for sound engineering students and The Irish Rock 'n' Roll Museum Experience, with much of its stock donated personally from Philomena Lynott, mother of the legendary Thin Lizzy frontman Phil Lynott. Still, it arrived with compromise. "We had wanted more than what we got – a 1000-capacity venue instead of 600-capacity, 22 rehearsal rooms instead of seven – but we took what we got," Dunning says.

stories.title: Martin McDonagh premieres Wild Horse Nine at Venice
stories.summary: Director Martin McDonagh has said his dark comedy Wild Horse Nine, ⁠which premiered at the Venice Film Festival on Thursday and centres on two CIA operatives before Chile's 1973 coup, feels unexpectedly relevant in today's turbulent world. The British-Irish filmmaker is known for crafting original stories that pair razor-sharp dialogue with bleak subject matter, including Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri and The Banshees of Inisherin, which opened at Venice in 2022. Watch: Martin McDonagh discusses the genesis of Wild Horse Nine at the Venice Film Festival McDonagh told Reuters he had not been thinking about current events when he wrote his latest script, but he now saw striking parallels between its themes and the present day. "It's almost the perfect time for a film like this to come out, because it points ⁠out that these things have been happening via the CIA or the nastier American governments for quite a while," he said. The 1973 Chilean coup followed covert US efforts to undermine President Salvador Allende.

stories.title: Conor Pope's tips for saving money at home this winter
stories.summary: "Generally speaking, winter is very expensive," says Pope, explaining that heating and lighting our homes in the colder, darker months adds up. Additionally, the need to tumble dry clothes can be a big expense, alongside buying warmer clothing, extra food, and saving up for Christmas presents. "I've done the maths, and I reckon that winter time costs about €10,000 more for the average household than summer time," he states. "That's not even being wildly extravagant." The first step in bringing those costs down? Shopping around for an electricity provider. "The reality is that more than 70% of Irish consumers don't switch their energy provider," the savvy saver explains, "despite the fact that, even in a climate of rising prices, you can still knock about €500 off your annual bill - just by moving from company A to company B." Many people will avoid switching because it feels like too much hassle, but Pope insists that sites like Bonkers.ie and Switcher.ie make it incredibly straightforward.

stories.title: Two trapped tunnel workers rescued in Nepal 'miracle'
stories.summary: Two hydropower workers have been pulled alive from a tunnel buried by debris in Nepal, a rare ray of hope on the tenth day of rescue efforts after catastrophic Himalayan flooding. Rescuers cheered as one man emerged through a muddy opening, a video released by the energy ministry showed. He was helped to his feet by rescuers, and later carried on the backs of the emergency workers, raising his hand as they took him towards a helicopter. A photograph showed the second man caked in mud, his hands pressed together in prayer, as rescuers brought him away on a stretcher. Rescuers called it a "miracle" after the disaster last week that has killed more than 1,300 people and left over 5,600 missing in Tibet and Nepal. "I am so happy, my heart is lighter," Amir Maharjan, the brother of rescued worker 45-year-old Kabir Maharjan, said.

stories.title: Hottest summer on record 'worrying to see'
stories.summary: Summer 2026 was the hottest ever recorded in Ireland, according to a provisional report from Met Éireann. While many people in the seaside town of Bray, Co Wicklow enjoyed the sunny days and hot weather, they also acknowledged that rising temperatures are cause for concern. "It's not being treated like an emergency at all and it's a bit sad to see it played-off as a nice thing." Aileen Maguire described it as a "beautiful summer" that she enjoyed with her family, but said it does make her worry about the future. "I worry for my grandchildren because I don't think it's going to be sustainable if the weather keeps heating up like this," she said. Ian Bolton said the summer temperatures did not worry him as he would "take bad winters if we get good summers".

stories.title: Taoiseach not ruling out cutting excise on alcohol
stories.summary: Taoiseach Micheál Martin has not ruled out cutting excise on alcohol as part of next month's Budget. The Government slashed the VAT rate for the hospitality sector as part of last year’s budget, with the rate for food services coming down to 9% from 13.5%. It was reported that a similar measure has been mooted to help pubs, as the cut in last year’s VAT rate applies only to food and non-alcoholic drinks. Mr Martin said that ministers have discussed income tax issues ahead of the Budget but have not moved into specific areas. "But of course, given the propensity of the industry itself to raise the cost of alcohol, in terms of the price of a pint, which varies in terms of locations, we will look at different sectors in the round," Mr Martin said. "Are there other mechanisms that can be used to support them? But that issue hasn’t surfaced at any talks we’ve had."

stories.title: Oil prices set for steepest weekly gain since mid-July
stories.summary: Oil prices rose today, heading for their steepest weekly gain since mid-July, as rising tension and renewed US-Iran hostilities heightened concerns over Middle East supply risks. Brent crude futures rose 54 cents, or 0.6%, to $96.06 a barrel early this morning, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures climbed 80 cents, or 0.9%, to $92.10. On a weekly basis, Brent rose 7.6% and WTI was 10.4% higher, set for the highest gains since the week ended July 20. US attacks this week that killed and wounded dozens, including Iranian civilians, marked the fiercest clashes between the two countries since July. The war, which began with US-Israeli strikes in late February, is now in its seventh month. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz renewed warnings that Israel would "cripple" Iran's military and civilian infrastructure, including energy facilities. ANZ analysts raised their Brent crude forecast on Friday to $95 a barrel in the short term, with upside risk if the Middle East conflict intensifies.

stories.title: Nepal toll rises to 1,252 as rescue operations continue
stories.summary: Catastrophic floods on the China-Nepal border have killed at least 1,252 people in Nepal, the disaster authority has said, taking overall deaths to more than 1,270. Chinese state media earlier confirmed 21 people were killed in Tibet, bringing the total toll from the disaster that struck on 26 August to 1,273. The number of missing in Nepal remained 4,216, as rescue operations continued on a war footing. In China, state media say there are 541 people missing, taking the overall number to 4,757. Nearly 600 foreigners from over 30 nationalities are also missing, with Indians making up one of the largest proportions. Some 75 Americans are also unaccounted for, according to the US State Department.

stories.title: O'Gara poised to sign new La Rochelle deal - report
stories.summary: Ronan O'Gara looks set to end speculation about his immediate future, with reports that he's close to signing a new contract with La Rochelle. The former Munster out-half and current La Rochelle head coach has been one of the standout candidates linked with succeeding Leo Cullen at Leinster. Cullen will step down from his role with Leinster at the end of the season and the province's chief executive Shane Nolan was coy when asked about the prospect of O'Gara replacing Cullen. O'Gara himself added fuel to the speculation in his Irish Examiner column last week. "The way some blue boys speak of you suggests I should be searching in my greying roots for devil horns in the morning," O'Gara wrote. "The Ronan O'Gara those lads remember from 20 years ago is not the coach of today, or indeed anything like him." In the same column he revealed that he had started conversations with La Rochelle about a contract extension, and now French sports outlet Midi Olympique is reporting the O'Gara is poised to sign a new four-year deal.

stories.title: Former referee Dean slammed for 'joking about' in games
stories.summary: Former Premier League referee Mike Dean invited a backlash after revealing he used to entertain himself by "joking about" and playing "games" while officiating top-flight matches. Dean, who refereed in 553 Premier League fixtures across more than two decades, made the confession during an appearance on the Jamie Vardy's Having a Party podcast. The 58-year-old, who retired in 2022 before a brief spell as a VAR assistant, told former England striker Vardy he would entertain himself by attempting not to use his whistle for as long as possible or by limiting his movement on the pitch. "There used to be games that we used to have, as a laugh, we used to say, something like 'we’ll kick off now, right? See how long we can go without blowing the whistle’," Dean said. "Done that a few times in the Premier League, before VAR obviously. Went 20 to 25 minutes without blowing a whistle a few times. Let it go, let it go, let it go. "I used to do another thing in the Premier League. I used to stand in the centre circle and see how long I could stay in the centre circle before I had to leave. That was just me joking about. But the lads used to be on the line saying ‘you can’t’. I said ‘I’ll try it’. I just used to kind of run around, kind of go, but don’t go out of it. Got (to) about 15 minutes once in one game, without leaving the centre circle." It is understood Dean’s claims have been met with bemusement by those with current involvement in officiating, with some noting a lack of factual detail in his stories.

stories.summary: Author Ronan McGreevy introduces his acclaimed book Seán Lemass: The Lost Memoir, a revealing portrait of the legendary politician, widely seen as a modernising force in Irish politics. Seán Lemass never left any papers or an autobiography. Instead, he gave 22 hours of interviews to an Irish businessman Dermot Ryan in 1967 and 1968. The transcripts were given to The Irish Times and extracts from these interviews were published as a supplement in May 2018. They laid bare tensions in his relationship with long standing Taoiseach de Valera, his disdain for the IRA, his complicated relationship with Great Britain and much more. In April 2022 a Sunday Independent/Ireland Thinks poll to mark the centenary of the State asked the Irish public who they believed to have been the best taoiseach. The clear winner was Seán Lemass, with 25.8 per cent of the vote. His nearest challenger was Fine Gael's Garret FitzGerald at 14.2 per cent. His record as taoiseach from 1959 to 1966 was such that even political opponents wondered what kind of Ireland would have emerged had he ascended to the role earlier in his career. The Labour Party leader Brendan Corish thought Lemass should have become taoiseach ten or fifteen years prior to 1959. 'It might have been a somewhat different Ireland’ – a view shared by the Fine Gael leader Liam Cosgrave when Lemass died in 1971. For all his achievements Lemass left no memoir or authorised biography in his lifetime. Neither did he donate his papers to a university, as many politicians have done. It was assumed he had no interest in giving his own version of events for posterity. This assumption is confounded by these recordings, which arose out of a series of 23 interviews between 22 April 1967 and 9 January1969 with the businessman Dermot Ryan. They are and were intended to be Lemass’s own take on his life in politics. Ryan, who was born in Dublin to a family from County Limerick, founded the Ryan Group, which had substantial interests in hotels, caravan parks, car hire and insurance in the 1950s and 1960s. He was also a member of the Fianna Fáil national executive and TACA, the party’s fundraising arm. He stood for election for Fianna Fáil in Dublin North-Central in the 1969 general election, but was unsuccessful. In a profile that year in The Irish Times his wealth was estimated at IR £2.5 million (€35 million today). He was a long-time admirer of Lemass and made him a member of the board of Ryan Tourism Holdings after Lemass retired as taoiseach in 1966. Ryan described Lemass as a man who could have been ‘a millionaire many times over if he had devoted his talents to business, but he and his contemporaries did not seem to care about money. I have never known a man with such intelligence, judgement and integrity as Lemass and who made such little money from his activities.’

stories.title: National Cinema Weekend: Tickets from €4 nationwide
stories.summary:
Cinema tickets will be available from €4 at participating cinemas across the country this weekend as National Cinema Weekend gets under way. Around 99% of cinemas will take part in the initiative on Saturday 5 and Sunday 6 September, with participating venues in every county. The event has been extended to two days this year following the success of previous National Cinema Days, which attracted more than 200,000 admissions in a single day. stories.title: Can stress really give you 'cortisol face'?
stories.summary: Social media is rife with discourse about 'cortisol face' and how to prevent it, but is it an actual medical complaint? Listen back to the full interview above. If you wake up with a puffy face, tired eyes and dull skin, you might have had a bad night's sleep. Or, if certain social media creators are to be believed, you're suffering from 'cortisol face'. The thoroughly online argument goes that consistent stress or burnout can lead to physical changes to your face and belly, including puffiness, swelling and rounded cheeks. However, Prof. Annie Curtis, Royal College of Surgeons of Ireland, joined Drivetime to debunk this beauty myth. "There's no such thing as cortisol face, it’s not a medical term. It’s absolutely rubbish, sorry about that." Cortisol, she explains, is one of many hormones created in the body, which act as "packages of information that are sent out from your glands to give information all around the body".

stories.title: Irish property prices overvalued by 17%, ESRI finds
stories.summary: Irish property prices are 17% overvalued, a new report from the Economic and Social Research Institute (ESRI) has found. The organisation measured house prices against a range of economic fundamentals including incomes, interest rates and demographics. The ESRI said while there was "a significant degree of overvaluation" it added it was "materially lower, and structurally different in nature, than the levels observed prior to the global financial crisis". It said the current situation represented an increase in the level of overvaluation since the most recent analysis using similar methods, which was published by the ESRI in December 2024. The ESRI added: "Unlike the pre-crisis period, which was driven by excessive credit growth and loose lending standards, the current episode of overvaluation appears to be primarily an affordability issue." It said house prices have risen faster than incomes, mortgage rates have increased, and not enough homes were being built to meet demand.

stories.title: Ambulances took over an hour on 20,000 occassions - FOI
stories.summary: Ambulances took more than an hour to respond to over 20,000 emergency calls in the past five years, new figures show. In some instances, patients were waiting around seven hours for an ambulance to arrive. Purple is the most serious and means there is a cardiac or respiratory arrest. Red relates to other life-threatening illnesses or injuries. The NAS aims to reach 75% of purple calls within 19 minutes and 45% of red calls within the same timeframe. But these figures reveal there were 20,244 occasions for the years 2021-2025 in which it took more than an hour for an ambulance to arrive. Forty-six of these were for purple calls, the highest level of emergency.

stories.title: Courts running 'effectively' amid aid dispute - minister
stories.summary: The Minister for Justice has said the criminal courts are running "effectively" amid an ongoing dispute with solicitors who have withdrawn their services. Jim O'Callaghan said he had made "very fair" concessions in amending his reforms of the criminal legal aid system which had prompted more than 100 solicitors to withdraw services. On 1 July, Minister O’Callaghan implemented a flat fee of €520 euro for criminal legal aid in the district court, rather than per-appearance fees, prompting anger and withdrawal of services among solicitors practising in the area. Previously, solicitors were given €240 euro for the first appearance and €60 euro on subsequent appearances. The new € 520 euro flat fee is equivalent to five appearances under the old system - which the minister argues is the average amount of appearances for criminal legal aid cases - plus an 8% increase in fees which was given to all criminal lawyers this year. Solicitors have been withdrawing their services from criminal cases where a person does not have the means to pay for a lawyer and requires legal aid.

stories.title: Around 100 jobs at risk at Daktronics in Co Clare
stories.summary: Around 100 jobs have been placed at risk at Daktronics in Ennistymon, Co Clare, as the US multinational begins a collective redundancy consultation. The company is considering withdrawing from its highly customised international transportation business, which supplies digital display and control systems to rail, bus and roadway customers outside the US and Canada. Daktronics said employees in Ireland have been informed that their positions are at risk as it consults with staff over the future of its Ennistymon manufacturing facility and other roles based in Ireland. In a statement, Daktronics said it was committed to engaging with employees "in good faith and in accordance with local employment laws" throughout the consultation process. Judd Guthmiller, Daktronics' vice president of international, described the proposal as a difficult decision, saying it reflected the challenges facing the market rather than the performance or commitment of its workforce. "We are committed to supporting our Ireland-based colleagues with transparency and respect throughout this process as we consider the future," he said.

stories.summary: Former champion boxer turned coach Andy Lee has said that Katie Taylor is a trailblazer who "makes you proud to be Irish" as she prepares to bow out in style in her farewell fight against Flora Pili at Croke Park on Saturday night. "She has to be focused and she'd want to go out with a bang", Lee said. "Just to go back to the first Chantelle Cameron fight, which when she lost, there was a big emotion because that was her homecoming. "That was her first time fighting here. She had a lot of emotion and she invested a lot of emotion in the ring walk. You remember she had the gospel music and she was quite internalised it seemed to me. "I think that played out in the fight I think so she has to be focused. There is jeopardy in this fight. "But she'd want to win the fight, just knowing her. She'll want to win and win it well."

stories.title: McDonald given permission to resume GAA club action
stories.summary: Mayo All-Ireland winner Kobe McDonald has been given the green light by AFL club St Kilda to play with his club Crossmolina for the remainder of their club championship campaign. The Deel Rovers side will be hoping to secure their spot in the knockout rounds when they face Mayo Gaels this weekend, and they should have their star youngster amongst their ranks. As reported by the Irish Examiner, McDonald, who had been given permission to remain with Mayo for the 2026 season after signing with the Melbourne club last November, and fellow Irish St Kilda players Eamonn Armstrong and Liam O'Connell will now line out with their clubs over the coming weeks. Armstrong plays with Duleek Bellewstown in Meath while O'Connell is a member of Ballincollig in Cork. McDonald headed to Australia days after Mayo’s famous All-Ireland final win over Kerry, but has been in Ireland recently and was on stage at Electric Picnic as members of the squad joined the Saw Doctors. "As a club, it's really important that we support our players in their lives outside of being professional AFL footballers," said Lenny Hayes, St Kilda's general manager of football.
